name: K'iche' Maya religion (Popol Vuh tradition, with Classic-period pan-Maya antecedents)

dating.dating_summary: The Popol Vuh's earliest surviving written form is Francisco Ximénez's 1701-1703 K'iche'/Spanish copy of a now-lost c. 1554-1558 alphabetic K'iche' original. The narrative content itself — the Hero Twins cycle, the Maize God's death and resurrection, the Lords of Xibalba — is independently attested in Classic-period (250-900 CE) painted ceramic iconography, pushing verified narrative antiquity back roughly a millennium before the earliest surviving manuscript, though the exact form and complexity of the pre-contact oral/pictorial tradition cannot be reconstructed with precision.

earliest_archaeological_evidence.note: Classic-period painted ceramics depict Hero Twins narrative scenes (Hunahpu and Xbalanque hunting with blowguns, descent into Xibalba) with enough narrative specificity/consistency that scholars (Michael Coe, "The Hero Twins: Myth and Image," in The Maya Vase Book Vol. 1, Kerr Associates, 1989; Karl Taube) treat the Popol Vuh's core narrative content as demonstrably pre-Columbian. This project already models an earlier Maya WritingSystem/Text pair (ws_maya_script, text_san_bartolo_murals, c. 300-200 BCE) documenting the writing system generally; that earliest writing does not itself carry identifiable Hero-Twins/creation narrative content, which is best attested later, in the Classic period proper.

earliest_written_attestation.note: The Classic-period corpus of painted ceramics carrying hieroglyphic captions alongside Hero Twins/Xibalba scenes (roughly 6th-9th c. CE) is pictorial-plus-glyphic, distinct from a continuous prose narrative in the modern sense; no earlier Maya text carrying identifiable Popol Vuh-type mythological content was located.

surviving_manuscript_date.note: Francisco Ximénez (Dominican friar, parish priest of Santo Tomás Chichicastenango), the only surviving copy of the K'iche' text with accompanying Spanish translation, held today at the Newberry Library, Chicago.

estimated_composition.method: Internal genealogical evidence: the text names Pedro de Robles as the reigning "Lord Magistrate" of the Nihaib lineage; de Robles is documented as taking office soon after 1554. Adrián Recinos (Popol Vuh: Las antiguas historias del Quiché, Fondo de Cultura Económica, 1947) and Dennis Tedlock (Popol Vuh: The Definitive Edition, Simon & Schuster, rev. ed. 1996) both independently proposed this window from that genealogical cross-reference. This is the lost c.1554-58 alphabetic K'iche' original Ximénez later copied — what became of it after copying is unknown.

tradition_internal_claim.note: The Popol Vuh presents itself internally as a re-writing/re-recording of an earlier sacred book that existed before the Spanish conquest and was lost or hidden; the K'iche' authors explicitly frame their 1550s text as reconstructing this earlier document from memory because "the original book... can no longer be seen" (per Tedlock's and Christenson's translations).

estimated_oral_origin.method: Classic-period iconographic evidence (Coe 1989; Taube) pushes verified narrative antiquity back roughly a millennium before the earliest surviving manuscript — see earliest_archaeological_evidence above; the exact pre-contact oral/pictorial form cannot be reconstructed precisely.

notes: Scope decision, explicit and sourced: "Maya" is not a single people (Matthew Restall, "Maya Ethnogenesis"; Sharer and Traxler, The Ancient Maya, 6th ed., Stanford UP, 2006) — this Tradition entity anchors specifically on K'iche' religion via the Popol Vuh, the best-documented Maya religious-narrative text, rather than claiming to represent a uniform pan-Maya religion; the underlying mythic figures (Hero Twins, Maize God, Xibalba) are attested far more broadly across the Classic Maya lowlands centuries before the K'iche' polity itself existed — the iconography is pan-Maya/Classic, the text is K'iche'/colonial. Contemporary K'iche' and broader highland Guatemalan Maya religious practice has documented restricted-knowledge/initiation conventions centered on the ajq'ij ("daykeeper") role, practitioners of the 260-day sacred calendar who undergo multi-year oral apprenticeship; ajq'ijab' practiced in secrecy during Guatemala's civil war (1960-1996) due to persecution, becoming more publicly visible only after the 1996 peace accords — reported here per the standing ethical constraint as existence-only, no restricted content described.
